evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of plastid presence/absence, as shown in Figure 1A, with citations to previous assumptions.

claim: This increases total known losses of plastid organelles in apicomplexans to three and in all eukaryotes to four.
source: This increases total known losses of plastid organelles in apicomplexans to three and in all eukaryotes to four (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the discovery of additional plastid losses, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Phylogenies of individual plastid genes repeatedly group Digyalum with apicomplexans and chrompodellids.
source: Firstly, phylogenies of individual plastid genes repeatedly group Digyalum with apicomplexans and chrompodellids, and their topologies either reiterate nuclear phylogenies directly or are unresolved without consistently supporting alternatives (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of individual plastid genes, as shown in Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Phylogenies of individual plastid genes either reiterate nuclear phylogenies directly or are unresolved without consistently supporting alternatives.
source: Firstly, phylogenies of individual plastid genes repeatedly group Digyalum with apicomplexans and chrompodellids, and their topologies either reiterate nuclear phylogenies directly or are unresolved without consistently supporting alternatives (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of individual plastid genes, as shown in Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unidentified lineages that carry plastid-encoded 16S rDNAs related to apicomplexans and chrompodellids (ARLs) are growing in number and diversity.
source: Secondly, unidentified lineages that carry plastid-encoded 16S rDNAs related to apicomplexans and chrompodellids (ARLs) are growing in number and diversity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the discovery of novel ARLs, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Some ARLs are apicomplexans and others may be free-living.
source: Some are apicomplexans (Janouškovec et al., 2013; Kwong et al., 2019) and others may be free-living, but they altogether support the idea that plastids in the lineage are widespread (Janouškovec et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying ARLs.

claim: ARLs altogether support the idea that plastids in the lineage are widespread.
source: Some are apicomplexans (Janouškovec et al., 2013; Kwong et al., 2019) and others may be free-living, but they altogether support the idea that plastids in the lineage are widespread (Janouškovec et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of ARLs, with a citation.

claim: Unique evolutionary innovations in the plastidial PREX, ispH, and hemH link together the plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum.
source: Finally, unique evolutionary innovations in the plastidial PREX, ispH, and hemH link together the plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum (bacterial fabG and split rpoC2 further link plastids in some of them).
evidence: This is based on the identification of shared innovations in plastid genes.

claim: Bacterial fabG and split rpoC2 further link plastids in some apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum.
source: Finally, unique evolutionary innovations in the plastidial PREX, ispH, and hemH link together the plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum (bacterial fabG and split rpoC2 further link plastids in some of them).
evidence: This is based on the identification of shared innovations in plastid genes.

claim: It is difficult to see how endosymbiosis would move plastids in or out of the lineage without changing the distribution of shared innovation genes.
source: It is difficult to see how endosymbiosis would move plastids in or out of the lineage without changing the distribution of these genes.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of shared innovations for plastid origin.

claim: The evidence suggests that plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum were inherited vertically from a common ancestor.
source: Altogether, the evidence suggests that plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum were inherited vertically from a common ancestor, are widely distributed in the group, and are most likely retained by default, particularly in free-living representatives (Janouškovec et al., 2015; Janouskovec et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and structural evidence, with citations.

claim: Plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum are widely distributed in the group.
source: Altogether, the evidence suggests that plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum were inherited vertically from a common ancestor, are widely distributed in the group, and are most likely retained by default, particularly in free-living representatives (Janouškovec et al., 2015; Janouskovec et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and structural evidence, with citations.

claim: Plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum are most likely retained by default, particularly in free-living representatives.
source: Altogether, the evidence suggests that plastids in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum were inherited vertically from a common ancestor, are widely distributed in the group, and are most likely retained by default, particularly in free-living representatives (Janouškovec et al., 2015; Janouskovec et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic and structural evidence, with citations.

claim: Core plastid metabolism in Digyalum, Symbiont X, and apicomplexans has been remarkably conserved across long time scales.
source: Core plastid metabolism in Digyalum, Symbiont X, and apicomplexans has been remarkably conserved across long time scales and reveals only a few outstanding variations.
evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid pathways.

claim: In Plasmodium falciparum, triose phosphate sugars are imported by two triose phosphate translocators (TPTs) residing in the outermost (PfoTPT) and innermost (PfiTPT) plastid membranes, respectively.
source: In Plasmodium falciparum, triose phosphate sugars are imported by two triose phosphate translocators (TPTs) residing in the outermost (PfoTPT) and innermost (PfiTPT) plastid membranes, respectively (Mullin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on TPTs.

claim: Toxoplasma contains only one TPT phylogenetically corresponding to PfoTPT.
source: Toxoplasma contains only one TPT phylogenetically corresponding to PfoTPT.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of TPTs.

claim: Orthologs of the PfoTPT lack N-terminal targeting signatures and are ubiquitous in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum.
source: Orthologs of the PfoTPT lack N-terminal targeting signatures and are ubiquitous in apicomplexans, chrompodellids, and Digyalum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TPT sequences, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PfiTPT orthologs are less common.
source: PfiTPT orthologs are less common (Gile and Slamovits, 2014), but they possess N-terminal signal peptides in Chromera, Vitrella, and Rhytidocystis sp. two compatible with their targeting to the inner plastid membrane (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TPT sequences, as shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2, with a citation.

claim: PfiTPT orthologs possess N-terminal signal peptides in Chromera, Vitrella, and Rhytidocystis sp. two compatible with their targeting to the inner plastid membrane.
source: PfiTPT orthologs are less common (Gile and Slamovits, 2014), but they possess N-terminal signal peptides in Chromera, Vitrella, and Rhytidocystis sp. two compatible with their targeting to the inner plastid membrane (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TPT sequences, as shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The split between the two TPT forms likely predated Apicomplexa.
source: The split between the two forms therefore likely predated Apicomplexa and the loss of the PfiTPT form in the lineage leading to Toxoplasma is apparently a derived evolutionary state.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of TPT forms.

claim: The loss of the PfiTPT form in the lineage leading to Toxoplasma is apparently a derived evolutionary state.
source: The split between the two forms therefore likely predated Apicomplexa and the loss of the PfiTPT form in the lineage leading to Toxoplasma is apparently a derived evolutionary state.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of TPT forms.

claim: The failure to identify TPI-II in piroplasms once led to the proposition that their plastids import glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, the TPI-II product.
source: One enzyme that processes the TPT substrate dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) is triose phosphate isomerase (TPI-II), and the failure to identify TPI-II in piroplasms once led to the proposition that their plastids import glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, the TPI-II product (Fleige et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: TPI-II, although highly divergent in piroplasms, is present in all apicomplexans with plastids.
source: We find that TPI-II, although highly divergent in piroplasms, is present in all apicomplexans with plastids, and it frequently possesses N-terminal signal peptides for plastid targeting (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the identification of TPI-II in transcriptomes, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TPI-II frequently possesses N-terminal signal peptides for plastid targeting.
source: We find that TPI-II, although highly divergent in piroplasms, is present in all apicomplexans with plastids, and it frequently possesses N-terminal signal peptides for plastid targeting (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TPI-II sequences, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The import and conversion of DHAP is conserved across apicomplexan plastids.
source: This suggests that the import and conversion of DHAP is conserved across apicomplexan plastids.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of TPI-II in all apicomplexans with plastids.

claim: The heme biosynthesis pathway consistently starts in the mitochondrion, as in heterotrophic eukaryotes.
source: Analysis of heme biosynthesis enzymes suggests that the pathway consistently starts in the mitochondrion, as in heterotrophic eukaryotes – the algal C5-pathway must have been lost prior to the Digyalum-Apicomplexa divergence.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization of heme biosynthesis enzymes.

claim: The algal C5-pathway must have been lost prior to the Digyalum-Apicomplexa divergence.
source: Analysis of heme biosynthesis enzymes suggests that the pathway consistently starts in the mitochondrion, as in heterotrophic eukaryotes – the algal C5-pathway must have been lost prior to the Digyalum-Apicomplexa divergence.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of the C5-pathway in both lineages.

claim: Delta-aminolevulinic acid is likely imported to the plastid and processed to coproporphyrinogen III.
source: Delta-aminolevulinic acid is likely imported to the plastid and processed to coproporphyrinogen III (Ralph et al., 2004; Sato et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on heme biosynthesis.

claim: The last three enzymes in heme biosynthesis in some apicomplexans are unexpectedly predicted to be plastidial, similarly to Chromera and Vitrella.
source: The last three enzymes in some apicomplexans sequenced by us are unexpectedly predicted to be also plastidial, similarly to Chromera and Vitrella (Koreny et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of protein localization, with a citation.

claim: In Plasmodium, and perhaps also in Toxoplasma and Digyalum, the last three heme biosynthesis enzymes localize in the cytosol and mitochondria, where heme is most needed.
source: In Plasmodium, and perhaps also in Toxoplasma and Digyalum, the last three heme biosynthesis enzymes localize in the cytosol and mitochondria, where heme is most needed (Varadharajan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on heme biosynthesis localization.

claim: It would be interesting to explore contrasting localization predictions experimentally, including the possibility that some enzymes are dually targeted, or their isoforms are differentially targeted to different cellular compartments.
source: It would be interesting to explore these contrasting localization predictions experimentally, including the possibility that some enzymes are dually targeted, or their isoforms (where present; Figure 2A) are differentially targeted to different cellular compartments.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the observed localization predictions, as shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Plastid genome structure shows unexpected variations across Apicomplexa.
source: Unlike metabolism in the plastid, plastid genome structure shows unexpected variations across Apicomplexa.
evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences.

claim: Plastid genomes in some of the newly sequenced taxa have unusually AT-rich and fast-evolving sequences.
source: Plastid genomes in some of the newly sequenced taxa, as partially reconstructed from transcripts, have unusually AT-rich and fast-evolving sequences (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of plastid genome sequences, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Completing the fragmentary plastid genome of Rhytidocystis species 2 is of particular interest because it has the most AT-rich 16S rDNA, and potentially the most AT-rich genome, ever recorded among plastids.
source: Completing the fragmentary plastid genome of Rhytidocystis species 2 (Supplementary file 7) is of particular interest because it has the most AT-rich 16S rDNA, and potentially the most AT-rich genome, ever recorded among plastids (Figure 3B) (Su et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AT content, as shown in Figure 3B, with a citation for comparison.

claim: Plastid genome reduction in Digyalum and Apicomplexa from their common ancestor is primarily explained by the loss of photosynthesis.
source: Plastid genome reduction in Digyalum and Apicomplexa from their common ancestor is primarily explained by the loss of photosynthesis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of plastid genome contents, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Plastid genome reduction was accompanied by relatively modest transfer of genes to the nucleus, which involved remarkably different gene sets in Digyalum and apicomplexan lineages.
source: This was accompanied by relatively modest transfer of genes to the nucleus, which involved remarkably different gene sets in the two lineages (only rps18 was relocated in both in parallel).
evidence: This is based on comparison of plastid genome contents.

claim: SufB encodes one of only two broadly conserved, plastid-encoded proteins with function other than transcribing and translating the genome itself.
source: Underlying the very existence of plastid DNA in Plasmodium and Toxoplasma is sufB, which encodes one of only two broadly conserved, plastid-encoded proteins with function other than transcribing and translating the genome itself.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of sufB.

claim: Of the newly sequenced species with plastids, only Symbiont X lacks any evidence for the sufB gene or plastid genome.
source: Of the newly sequenced species with plastids, only Symbiont X lacks any evidence for the sufB gene or plastid genome (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on the absence of sufB and plastid genome sequences in the transcriptome, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: It would be expected that Symbiont X sufB is encoded in the nucleus and was relocated there in its common ancestor with Chromera, Voromonas, Colpodella, and Alphamonas.
source: It would be expected that Symbiont X sufB is encoded in the nucleus and was relocated there in its common ancestor with Chromera, Voromonas, Colpodella, and Alphamonas (Janouškovec et al., 2015), thus allowing heterotrophs in this lineage to lose plastid genomes at least three times independently (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of sufB in the plastid genome and the phylogenetic position of Symbiont X, as shown in Figure 5, with a citation.

claim: Heterotrophs in the lineage including Symbiont X lost plastid genomes at least three times independently.
source: It would be expected that Symbiont X sufB is encoded in the nucleus and was relocated there in its common ancestor with Chromera, Voromonas, Colpodella, and Alphamonas (Janouškovec et al., 2015), thus allowing heterotrophs in this lineage to lose plastid genomes at least three times independently (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of plastid genomes in multiple species, as shown in Figure 5.

claim: A strongly resolved phylogeny and large-scale sequence data for major apicomplexan groups are provided.
source: We provide a strongly resolved phylogeny and large-scale sequence data for major apicomplexan groups, but the sampling of Apicomplexa is far from complete.
evidence: This summarizes the main contribution of the study.

claim: The sampling of Apicomplexa is far from complete.
source: We provide a strongly resolved phylogeny and large-scale sequence data for major apicomplexan groups, but the sampling of Apicomplexa is far from complete.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Expanding the phylogenetic dataset with new species and genes will allow for testing key conclusions of the study.
source: Expanding the phylogenetic dataset with new species and genes will allow for testing key conclusions of our study (e.g., monophyly of gregarines and eugregarines) and understanding the relationships of taxa that remain poorly sampled (archigregarines, blastogregarines, protococcidians) or lack genome-level sequences (corralicolids, adeleid and aggregatid coccidians, and other incertae sedis taxa).
